title: 08. Microservices & Architecture Patterns: Microservices Architecture — chapter overview
summary: Microservices is an architectural pattern where an application is split into small, independent services, each responsible for a single business capability.

sections.title: Detailed Explanation
sections.body:
### What are Microservices?

**Microservices** is an architectural pattern where an application is split into small, independent services, each responsible for a single business capability. Each service runs in its own process, has its own database, and communicates via lightweight protocols (HTTP/gRPC).

### Monolith vs Microservices

| Aspect            | Monolith            | Microservices             |
| ----------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Deployment        | Single unit         | Independent per service   |
| Scaling           | Scale entire app    | Scale individual services |
| Technology        | Single tech stack   | Polyglot (mix languages)  |
| Database          | Shared database     | Database per service      |
| Team structure    | One large team      | Small autonomous teams    |
| Failure isolation | One bug crashes all | Isolated blast radius     |
| Complexity        | Simple at start     | Complex infrastructure    |
| Testing           | Simple integration  | Complex E2E testing       |

### Key Microservice Principles

1. **Single Responsibility** — One service, one business capability
2. **Loose Coupling** — Services know minimal about each other
3. **High Cohesion** — Related logic grouped together
4. **Independent Deployment** — Deploy without affecting others
5. **Decentralized Data** — Each service owns its data
6. **Design for Failure** — Expect services to fail

diagrams.title: A typical microservices layout
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  c["Clients"] --> gw["API gateway: auth, rate limit, routing"]
  gw --> us["User service"]
  gw --> os["Order service"]
  gw --> ps["Product service"]
  us --> udb[("users DB")]
  os --> odb[("orders DB")]
  ps --> pdb[("products DB")]
  os -->|"events"| k[["Kafka"]]
  k --> ns["Notification service"]
  reg["Service discovery"] -.-> us
  reg -.-> os
  reg -.-> ps
diagrams.explain: Each service owns one business capability **and its own database**, so teams deploy and scale independently. An **API gateway** is the single front door; **service discovery** lets services find each other; asynchronous events decouple workflows. The trade: network calls fail, data is spread out, and you need tracing, circuit breakers and good automation — a monolith is often the right start.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Monolith vs Microservices

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               MONOLITH → MICROSERVICES EVOLUTION                            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  MONOLITH:                        MICROSERVICES:
  ┌─────────────────────────┐      ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐
  │     Single Application  │      │ User   │ │ Order  │ │Product │
  │                         │      │Service │ │Service │ │Service │
  │  ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐       │      │  🐍    │ │  ☕    │ │  🔷    │
  │  │User │ │Order│       │      │ Python │ │ Java   │ │ Go     │
  │  │Logic│ │Logic│       │      ├────────┤ ├────────┤ ├────────┤
  │  └─────┘ └─────┘       │      │  DB 1  │ │  DB 2  │ │  DB 3  │
  │  ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐       │      └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘
  │  │ Pay │ │Notif│       │           │          │          │
  │  │Logic│ │Logic│       │      ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐
  │  └─────┘ └─────┘       │      │Payment │ │Notif.  │ │Search  │
  │                         │      │Service │ │Service │ │Service │
  ├─────────────────────────┤      │  🔷    │ │  🐍    │ │  🔷    │
  │    SHARED DATABASE      │      │ Go     │ │ Python │ │ Rust   │
  └─────────────────────────┘      ├────────┤ ├────────┤ ├────────┤
                                   │  DB 4  │ │  DB 5  │ │  DB 6  │
  → One codebase                   └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘
  → One deployment
  → One database                   → Independent codebases
  → Scale everything together      → Independent deployments
                                   → Separate databases
                                   → Scale individually
```

### Microservices Communication Patterns

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                COMMUNICATION PATTERNS                                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  1. SYNCHRONOUS (Request/Response):
     ┌────────┐  HTTP/gRPC  ┌────────┐
     │Service │ ──────────▶│Service │  Waits for response
     │   A    │ ◀──────────│   B    │  Strong coupling
     └────────┘  response   └────────┘  Cascading failures possible

  2. ASYNCHRONOUS (Event/Message):
     ┌────────┐  publish    ┌─────────┐  consume  ┌────────┐
     │Service │ ──────────▶│ Message │ ─────────▶│Service │
     │   A    │             │  Queue  │           │   B    │
     └────────┘             └─────────┘           └────────┘
     Fire and forget — loosely coupled — resilient

  3. CHOREOGRAPHY (Event-Driven):
     ┌──────┐  order.created  ┌──────┐  payment.done  ┌──────┐
     │Order │ ──────────────▶│  Pay │ ──────────────▶│ Ship │
     └──────┘   (event bus)   └──────┘   (event bus)   └──────┘
     No central coordinator — services react to events

  4. ORCHESTRATION (Saga):
     ┌──────────────┐
     │ Orchestrator │ ──▶ Step 1: Create Order
     │              │ ──▶ Step 2: Process Payment
     │              │ ──▶ Step 3: Reserve Inventory
     │              │ ──▶ Step 4: Ship Order
     │              │
     │  On failure: │ ──▶ Compensate in reverse
     └──────────────┘
```

### Service Discovery

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   SERVICE DISCOVERY                                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  CLIENT-SIDE DISCOVERY:
  ┌──────┐  1. Query     ┌──────────────┐
  │Client│ ──────────▶  │  Service     │  Registry knows all
  │      │ ◀──────────  │  Registry    │  service instances
  │      │  2. Get IPs   │ (Consul/etcd)│
  │      │               └──────────────┘
  │      │  3. Call directly
  │      │ ──────────────────────────────▶ Service Instance
  └──────┘

  SERVER-SIDE DISCOVERY:
  ┌──────┐  1. Request   ┌──────────────┐  2. Forward  ┌──────────┐
  │Client│ ──────────▶  │ Load Balancer│ ──────────▶ │ Service  │
  │      │               │ (knows all   │              │ Instance │
  └──────┘               │  instances)  │              └──────────┘
                         └──────────────┘
                               │ Queries
                               ▼
                         ┌──────────────┐
                         │   Registry   │
                         └──────────────┘
```

### Circuit Breaker Pattern

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   CIRCUIT BREAKER STATE MACHINE                             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

                    success
         ┌──────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                              │
  ┌──────────────┐   failure count    ┌─┴───────────┐
  │    CLOSED    │   > threshold      │  HALF-OPEN  │
  │ (normal flow)│──────────────────▶ │ (test one   │
  │              │                    │  request)   │
  └──────────────┘                    └─────────────┘
         ▲                              │
         │              failure         │
         │         ┌──────────────┐     │
         │         │    OPEN      │◀────┘
         └─────────│ (reject all  │
      timeout      │  requests)   │
      expires      │  Return fast │
                   │  error/fallback│
                   └──────────────┘

  States:
  CLOSED  → Normal operation, requests pass through
  OPEN    → All requests fail immediately (fast fail)
  HALF-OPEN → Allow one test request to check if service recovered
```

quiz.question: What are microservices and when should you use them?
options: Solves: how to atomically update database AND publish an event.
Single entry point for all clients.
In dynamic environments (containers/cloud), service instances change frequently.
Use when: team is large (>20 devs), need independent deployment cycles, different scaling needs per feature, need technology diversity.
quiz.explanation: Microservices split an application into small, independently deployable services, each owning a business capability and database. Use when: team is large (>20 devs), need independent deployment cycles, different scaling needs per feature, need technology diversity. DON'T use for: small teams, simple applications, early-stage startups (start with monolith, extract later).

quiz.explanation: eventual consistency** — services will converge to consistent state. Techniques: (1) Saga pattern for distributed transactions, (2) Event sourcing — events as source of truth, (3) CQRS — separate read/write models, (4) Outbox pattern — write event + data in same local transaction, (5) Change Data Capture (CDC) — capture database changes as events.
